Reliability and Item Analysis Tables

Source: vignettes/articles/reliability.qmd 
library(apa7)
library(psych)

apa_reliability reports useful aspects of a reliability analysis. For each item, it shows:

  • the mean (M) and standard deviation (SD), which reveal ceiling and floor effects
  • the corrected item–total correlation (rit), the item’s correlation with the sum of the other items in its scale. Items with low values (often, below .30) discriminate poorly.
  • Cronbach’s α if the item were deleted. A value above the scale’s α means that the item lowers reliability.

Below each scale’s items are its scale-level statistics: the mean and SD of the scale scores, Cronbach’s α with a confidence interval, McDonald’s ωtotal, and the mean inter-item correlation. Cronbach’s α assumes that all items are equally good measures of what the scale measures, while ωtotal allows them to differ, so many journals now ask for both. The mean inter-item correlation shows whether a high α comes from strongly related items or merely from many items.

The statistics come from the psych package: psych::alpha for α and the item statistics, and a one-factor model (psych::fa) for ωtotal. The confidence interval of α is Feldt’s.

Several Scales

The bfi data set in the psych package has 25 personality items from 2,800 people, answered on a 6-point scale. Give apa_reliability a named list of scales, each a vector of item names. Items worded in the opposite direction (e.g., A1, “Am indifferent to the feelings of others”) are reverse-scored with reverse. item_range gives the lowest and highest possible responses, which are used to reverse the items:

bfi_scales <- list(
  Agreeableness = paste0("A", 1:5),
  Conscientiousness = paste0("C", 1:5)
)
bfi_reverse <- c("A1", "C4", "C5")

apa_reliability(
  bfi,
  scales = bfi_scales,
  reverse = bfi_reverse,
  item_range = c(1, 6)
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Scale scores are the means of the items. rit = corrected item–total correlation (the correlation of the item with the sum of the other items); α if deleted = Cronbach’s α without the item; α = Cronbach’s α; CI = 95% confidence interval (Feldt et al., 1987); ωtotal = McDonald’s ωtotal (McDonald, 1999) from a one-factor model.

Each scale has a heading, with its items and statistics indented below it. Reverse-scored items are marked (R). Each scale uses the respondents who answered all of its items, and the note gives their number.

A1 has the weakest item–total correlation of the agreeableness items, and deleting it would raise α slightly, from .70 to .72. With flag = TRUE, item–total correlations below .30 (or another cutoff, with min_item_total) and values of α if deleted that exceed the scale’s α are bolded:

apa_reliability(
  bfi,
  scales = bfi_scales,
  reverse = bfi_reverse,
  item_range = c(1, 6),
  flag = TRUE
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

One Row per Scale

When the items have been examined and the paper reports only the scales, level = "scales" gives one row per scale. This table pairs naturally with a correlation table of the scale scores (see apa_cor).

apa_reliability(
  bfi,
  scales = list(
    Agreeableness = paste0("A", 1:5),
    Conscientiousness = paste0("C", 1:5),
    Extraversion = paste0("E", 1:5),
    Neuroticism = paste0("N", 1:5),
    Openness = paste0("O", 1:5)
  ),
  reverse = c("A1", "C4", "C5", "E1", "E2", "O2", "O5"),
  item_range = c(1, 6),
  level = "scales"
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Test Items Scored 0 or 1

For tests whose items are scored correct (1) or incorrect (0), M is the item’s difficulty (the proportion of correct answers), rit is the corrected point-biserial correlation, and α equals the Kuder–Richardson formula 20 (KR-20). apa_reliability detects such items and says so in the table and the note. Here, 300 simulated students answered 6 items of increasing difficulty:

set.seed(1)
ability <- rnorm(300)
difficulty <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = 6)
test_items <- sapply(difficulty, \(b) rbinom(300, 1, plogis(ability - b)))
colnames(test_items) <- paste0("Item", 1:6)

apa_reliability(as.data.frame(test_items)) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Items are scored 0 or 1: for these, M is item difficulty (the proportion of 1s), rit is the corrected point-biserial correlation, and α equals KR-20. rit = corrected item–total correlation (the correlation of the item with the sum of the other items); α if deleted = Cronbach’s α without the item; α = Cronbach’s α; CI = 95% confidence interval (Feldt et al., 1987); ωtotal = McDonald’s ωtotal (McDonald, 1999) from a one-factor model.

With a single scale, there is no scale heading. Six items of modest discrimination give a low KR-20; longer tests are usually needed for dependable scores.

Options

  • omega = FALSE leaves out ωtotal.
  • score = "sum" reports the mean and SD of the scale sums instead of the scale means.
  • ci sets the confidence level of the interval of α (e.g., ci = .90).
  • format_variable_names = FALSE keeps item and scale names exactly as they are.
